title: How {language} looks
summary: Its alphabet, the letters that are new to you, and the marks that change how words sound.

marks.title: Marks that matter
marks.body: Small signs on or around letters. They can change a sound or show where the stress goes.

complete.title: Now you know what to look for
complete.body: Gef is already squinting at street signs.

labels.script.has_case: It has capital and small letters.
labels.letters.shared: {shared} of its {total} letters are in {known} too.
labels.letters.all_shared: Every letter is one you already know.
labels.letters.none_shared: It has {total} letters, and none of them are shared with {known}.
labels.letters.none_new: Nothing new here: every letter is already in {known}.
labels.letters.lookalike_body: These look like letters you know, but they sound different.
labels.markrole.pronounce_vowel: Tells you to pronounce a vowel you might skip.
labels.markrole.vowel_quality: Changes the quality of the vowel.
labels.punctuation.title: Punctuation
labels.q.new_letter: Which of these is a letter you won’t find in {known}?
labels.q.match_letters: Match each letter to a word that uses it.
labels.kind.alphabet: {layer} is an alphabet: each letter stands for a sound.
labels.kind.abjad: {layer} is an abjad: it spells out the consonants and mostly leaves the vowels for the reader to fill in.
labels.kind.abugida: {layer} is an abugida: each symbol is a consonant with a vowel built in, and marks change the vowel.
labels.kind.syllabary: {layer} is a syllabary: each symbol stands for a whole syllable.
labels.kind.logographic: {layer} is a character system: each character stands for a word or a piece of a word, not for a sound, so you learn them one by one.
labels.kind.featural: {layer} is built from shapes that show how each sound is made.
labels.kind.romanization: {layer} spells the sounds with Latin letters, so you can read and say words before you know the characters.
labels.layer.also.aid: {language} also uses {layer} beside it, to help you read and say the words.
labels.direction.opposite: It runs {direction}: the other way round from {base}.
labels.joined.true: Letters join up, and each one changes shape depending on where it sits in a word.
labels.vowels.marks_optional: Short vowels are usually not written. Small marks can show them when they are needed.
labels.vowels.inherent: Every consonant carries a built-in vowel unless a mark changes it.
labels.characters.title: Characters to know
labels.characters.body: A few common ones. Each is a word, or a piece of one.
labels.mark.fatha: fatha (a small slanted stroke above a letter)
labels.mark.kasra: kasra (a small slanted stroke below a letter)
labels.mark.damma: damma (a tiny curl above a letter)
labels.mark.sukun: sukun (a tiny circle above a letter)
labels.mark.shadda: shadda (a tiny w-shape above a letter)
labels.mark.tanwin: tanwin (a doubled mark at the end of a noun)
labels.markrole.short_vowel: Writes a short vowel, which the letters alone don’t show.
labels.markrole.no_vowel: Shows that no vowel follows the letter.
labels.markrole.doubling: Shows that the sound is doubled, held about twice as long.
labels.markrole.case_ending: Adds an -n ending (-un, -an or -in) to a noun and shows its role in the sentence.
labels.layer.hanzi.note: Chinese is written with two sets of characters. Simplified characters are standard in mainland China and Singapore. Traditional characters, the older and more detailed forms, are used in Taiwan and Hong Kong. This lesson shows simplified characters.
labels.layer.pinyin.note: Pinyin spells Chinese sounds with Latin letters and small tone marks. It helps you read and say new words. Everyday writing uses characters.
labels.markrole.tone: Shows which tone the syllable is said in.
labels.q.match_readings: Match each character to how it’s read.

glosses.ar:writing.arabic.example.semicolon: I am a student; he is a teacher.
